justification_text:
The point estimates for each time horizon—1 day, 1 week, and 1 month—reflect a baseline or central expectation of 56.54 for the variable being forecasted. These point estimates likely came from a model that assumes stability in the short term, with an equal balance of upward and downward forces over time. In simpler terms, the forecast is grounded on an assumption that recent trends, historical data, or averages will persist in the near future without any notable disruptions. Therefore, the point estimate remains the same across all three horizons because, on average, no major directional shift is expected.

The widths of the confidence intervals (CIs) grow as the time horizon extends because uncertainty tends to increase the further out you forecast. Over 1 day, variability is expected to be relatively small, as fewer intervening factors can significantly alter the situation in such a short period. By the time you look one week or one month ahead, there are more opportunities for unexpected events, random fluctuations, or compounding errors in the forecast model to introduce variability. This is why the 90% CI starts narrow (55.98 to 57.1 for 1 day) and becomes progressively wider for 1 week (54.9 to 58.18) and 1 month (53.0 to 60.08).

Risks or specific events could still push the outcomes outside these confidence intervals, though the forecast accounts for a range of typical variability. Sudden shocks or unexpected developments—such as political announcements, economic surprises, supply chain disruptions, or natural disasters—could create outcomes beyond the "90% confidence" range. For instance, if the variable being forecast is stock market performance, a surprise interest rate hike or a major geopolitical conflict could cause sharp deviations. However, in the absence of these extreme events, the probabilities suggest a high likelihood that the outcomes will fall within the calculated intervals.
